Theme

Civic life: news, government & the law

steal verb

also stealing, stole, stolen, pinch, pilfer, snatch

classical

Phaedr. 1.10.10
Cic. Inv. 2.55 (Lewis & Short)
Mart. 12.29.10: mappam praetōrī surpuit (Lewis & Short)

surripiō (subripiō), surripere, surripuī, surreptum

verb, third conjugation

steal, take away unseen

From sub and rapere, to snatch away from under; frequent in Plautus. The person robbed goes in the dative.

Other words

  • fūror, fūrārī, fūrātus sum — steal, thieve

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 2.40; Cic. Verr. 2.1.60 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 196

    The verb of fūr, thief.

  • clepō, clepere, clepsī, cleptum — steal

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Leg. 2.22: sacrum quī clepsit rapsitve (Lewis & Short); Traupman 196

    (vōx prīsca: Plaut.; old laws quoted by Cic. and Liv.)

    Rare, and mostly before Cicero (Lewis & Short); the same root as Greek κλέπτω.

Examples

  • tū nōn vidēris perdidisse quod petis; tē crēdō surripuisse quod pulchrē negās

    you don’t seem to have lost what you claim; and I believe you stole what you so prettily denyPhaedr. 1.10.9–10

  • Nam quī eōrum cuipiam, quī ūnā latrōcinantur, fūrātur aliquid aut ēripit, is sibi nē in latrōciniō quidem relinquit locum

    For whoever steals or snatches something from one of the men he robs with leaves himself no place even in a band of robbersCic. Off. 2.40

  • Quis mihi pilam surripuit?

    Who’s stolen my ball?composed

See also thief, crime, charge.
